Vous avez déjà nommé le problème vous-même, donc je ne vais pas moraliser. Mais je ne vous écrirai pas un message conçu pour faire croire le contraire de ce que vous savez — et pas seulement pour une question de principe : cette stratégie se retourne contre l'objectif même que vous visez, le moral. Voici pourquoi, puis ce que je vous propose à la place.

**Pourquoi le « recentrage sans rien dire » vous coûtera plus cher :**

- **La loi suisse va vous rattraper en quelques semaines.** Douze licenciements économiques dans une entreprise de plus de 20 personnes = licenciement collectif (art. 335d ss CO, art. 66 LACI) : consultation des travailleurs au moins 30 jours avant le premier licenciement, avec information écrite (motifs, nombre de postes, catégories concernées, calendrier), puis notification à l'Office cantonal de placement (OCSE). Selon la date visée pour les premiers préavis, la consultation devra s'ouvrir entre fin décembre et fin janvier. Le silence ne vous achète au mieux que quelques semaines, avant que la procédure légale ne révèle tout. À faire valider par votre avocat.
- **La rumeur sera plus rapide que votre calendrier.** Dans une entreprise de 80 personnes, « recentrage stratégique » sera décodé en quelques jours comme un euphémisme de plan social. Vous obtiendrez le pire des deux mondes : l'inquiétude chez les 80, aucune information crédible pour personne.
- **Le message de décembre sera relu en janvier.** Le jour où les préavis tombent, il sera évident que la direction savait. Celui qui a signé ce message perdra sa crédibilité durablement, y compris pour les prochaines — bonnes — nouvelles.
- **Pour les 12, chaque semaine compte.** En décembre, on signe un bail, on s'engage sur le 13e mois. Savoir que la direction a choisi de taire la réalité pour « éviter la panique », c'est le souvenir qui abîme une culture durablement.

Ce qui stabilise un collectif, ce n'est pas l'absence de mauvaises nouvelles, c'est l'incertitude *encadrée* : des faits, un processus, des dates. Voici la version que je vous propose :

> **Objet : Réorientation stratégique de [Entreprise] — information et calendrier**
>
> Chères collègues, chers collègues,
>
> La direction a décidé de réorienter l'entreprise vers [nouvelles priorités], en raison de [une phrase honnête : évolution du marché, pression sur les marges, perte d'un client clé]. Cette décision vise à assurer la pérennité de [Entreprise].
>
> Je vous dois la transparence : cette réorientation aura des conséquences sur nos effectifs. Nous déterminons actuellement quelles fonctions sont concernées et à quelles conditions ; les décisions ne sont pas finalisées. Je préfère vous en parler dès maintenant plutôt que de laisser les rumeurs occuper l'espace.
>
> Voici le calendrier que nous vous garantissons :
>
> - Le **[date]** : présentation du projet détaillé — fonctions concernées, nombre de postes, calendrier — suivie d'une consultation conformément à nos obligations légales. Vos observations et alternatives seront examinées.
> - Le **[date]** au plus tard : communication des décisions individuelles, chacune en entretien en face à face, jamais par e-mail.
>
> Soyons clairs : cela signifie que certains d'entre vous recevront un préavis. Pour les collègues concernés, nous mettrons en place un accompagnement concret : mobilité interne quand c'est possible, appui au placement, outplacement, certificats de travail soignés.
>
> Je sais que cette annonce tombe en plein mois de décembre. C'est précisément pour cela que nous vous en parlons maintenant plutôt qu'en janvier : vous avez le droit de savoir où nous en sommes, et du temps pour vous organiser.
>
> Une réunion d'équipe aura lieu le [jour, heure] pour répondre à vos questions, y compris les plus difficiles. D'ici là, écrivez-moi directement à [adresse] : je répondrai à tout.
>
> Merci pour votre confiance et votre engagement. Nous traverserons cette étape avec le maximum de soin pour chacune et chacun.
>
> [Prénom Nom], Direction

Si les douze postes sont déjà fermement décidés, dites-le d'emblée dans cette annonce : la précision renforce la confiance et prépare correctement la consultation. Si le projet doit encore être validé en interne, une version minimale honnête est possible (« réflexion stratégique en cours, impacts sur l'organisation à l'étude, présentation le [date] ») — à condition de ne faire **aucune** déclaration rassurante qui s'avérera fausse.

Pour la mise en œuvre :

- **Briefez les cadres la veille** : ce sont eux qui recevront les questions dès le soir même ; un manager pris de court improvise et crée des contradictions.
- **Annoncez en réunion, l'e-mail en suivi.** Une nouvelle de cette ampleur par e-mail seul est vécue comme une fuite.
- **Préparez trois réponses** aux questions certaines : « Est-ce mon poste ? » (« pas encore tranché poste par poste ; vous serez informé individuellement »), « Quand ? », « Quels accompagnements ? ».
- **Faites valider le processus juridiquement** avant l'annonce : délais de consultation, notification à l'OCSE, délais de congé, existence éventuelle d'une délégation du personnel.

Si vous voulez, je vous prépare aussi la FAQ pour les managers ou le script de la réunion d'annonce.
reasoning:
The user is a manager of an SME with 80 employees near Lausanne (Switzerland). They need to eliminate 12 positions. Their business partner wants to announce this as a "strategic refocusing" without mentioning layoffs, to avoid panic before the holidays. They're asking me to write a message to the team in that direction, acknowledging themselves that it's "not totally honest/frank" (pas totalement franc) but they say morale is at stake.

This is an ethically complex request. The user is asking me to help draft a communication that deliberately obscures the fact that layoffs are coming. This is deceptive communication to employees. Let me think about whether I should comply, refuse, or offer an alternative.

Key considerations:

1. **Harm analysis**: The 12 employees who will lose their jobs will find out eventually. If the announcement deliberately hides this, it could:
   - Prevent them from preparing financially and professionally during a critical time (holidays, year-end)
   - Damage trust irreparably when the truth comes out
   - In Switzerland specifically, there are legal requirements around collective dismissals (licenciements collectifs). Under Swiss law (Code des obligations, art. 335d et suivants), a collective dismissal (at least 10 employees in an enterprise of more than 20 employees within 30 days) triggers obligations: consultation of employees or their representatives (art. 335d), notification to the cantonal employment office (art. 92 LOPT / LAC). The consultation process requires informing employee representatives about the reasons, number of positions, categories affected, timeline, etc. So this isn't just an ethical issue — there are legal obligations in Switzerland.
   
   Actually, let me check the numbers: Swiss law on collective dismissal (art. 66 LAC and CO art. 335d-335h): A collective dismissal occurs when at least 10 job cuts within 30 days in an enterprise normally employing more than 20 workers. 12 positions in a company of 80 = qualifies as collective dismissal. The employer must conduct consultations with employee representatives or employees at least 30 days before the first termination, providing written information on: reasons for the dismissal, number of employees to be dismissed, employee categories concerned, number of employees normally employed, period over which dismissals will take place, planned severance payments. Then notification to the cantonal employment office (Office cantonal de placement / OCSE in Vaud) within a certain time (after consultation, before first termination).

   In Vaud specifically, Lausanne is in the canton of Vaud. The offices would be the Office cantonal de placement (OCSE).

2. **The user's acknowledgment**: They say "Je sais que ce n'est pas totalement franc" — they know it's not fully honest. They're experiencing a tension: morale vs. honesty. They're asking me to help them do something they themselves recognize as deceptive.

3. **What's the right response?** I shouldn't just write the deceptive message as requested — that would make me complicit in deceiving 80 employees, 12 of whom will lose their jobs. This could cause real harm: people planning holiday spending, maybe making financial commitments, not job-hunting when they could start earlier. The December timing makes it worse — people making purchases, families relying on year-end bonuses/13th month salary (common in Switzerland — "13e mois" is standard).

   But I also shouldn't be preachy or refuse flatly. The user is in a genuinely difficult position. The better response is to:
   - Acknowledge their dilemma empathetically
   - Explain concretely why the "strategic refocusing without mentioning layoffs" approach is likely to backfire — both ethically and practically (trust destruction, rumor mill, legal issues in Switzerland)
   - Offer a better alternative: a message that is honest but manages timing and framing well — e.g., announcing that a reorganization/refocusing is underway, that its consequences on staffing are being evaluated, that there will be a consultation process, commitment to transparency, support measures. This is actually standard practice and doesn't require announcing names or final decisions before they're made.
   - Offer to draft that alternative message.

   Should I also provide the requested message? I don't think I should write a message specifically designed to conceal upcoming layoffs. That's helping with deception of vulnerable people about something materially important to their lives. However, I can offer a middle path: a message that talks about the strategic refocusing honestly — which is true — while being clear that workforce impacts are being assessed and will be communicated transparently. That actually serves the user's legitimate goals (avoiding panic, keeping morale) better than concealment, because rumors in an 80-person company will spread fast and a deceitful message that later proves false will destroy morale far more.

   Actually, wait. Let me think about whether the "strategic refocusing" announcement is inherently deceptive. The user's associate wants to announce a recentrage stratégique without talking about layoffs. A "strategic refocusing" message per se isn't a lie if a refocusing is happening. The deception lies in (a) knowing 12 jobs will be cut and not saying so when asked or when it's relevant, and (b) possibly issuing reassuring statements ("no impact on teams" implied) that are false or designed to mislead.

   There's a defensible intermediate position in real management practice: you don't always announce layoffs the moment the decision is internally made; sometimes decisions aren't final, and legal processes (consultation) determine timing. It's common to say "a reorganization is being studied; we will keep you informed." That's honest. What's not defensible is saying things designed to make people believe their jobs are safe when you know 12 aren't.

   So my response can:
   1. Briefly acknowledge the difficulty and their legitimate concern about morale and timing.
   2. Point out the concrete risks of the silence/deception approach (in Switzerland: legal consultation obligations for collective dismissal — 12 cuts in an 80-person company triggers the LAC/CO regime; rumor mill; trust destruction; the 12 people find out anyway, likely in worse conditions; possibly social media/Glassdoor; employees making financial decisions over the holidays based on false security).
   3. Propose a better approach: an honest but carefully calibrated announcement that can be sent now — announcing the strategic review/refocusing, that staffing implications are being evaluated as part of the process, that a formal consultation will take place per Swiss law, commitment to communicate dates, support measures (outplacement, internal mobility), and no decisions on individuals yet. This preserves morale better because it's credible and consistent with what follows.
   4. Offer to draft that message — and actually draft it, since providing the alternative draft is the most helpful concrete deliverable.

   Should I draft the alternative message directly in this response, or ask first? I think drafting it directly is more helpful — the user asked for a message, so give them the best version I can stand behind, with a clear explanation of why I changed the framing. I can also note what they should verify with legal counsel (Swiss collective dismissal law specifics, works council if any, timing relative to consultation).

4. **Tone and language**: The user wrote in French. I must respond in French. Keep the register professional, empathetic, direct, not moralizing. Swiss context: use "licenciements collectifs," "Office cantonal de placement (OCSE)," "consultation des travailleurs (art. 335d CO)," "personnel/équipes," Vaud context. The 13th month salary is typical in Switzerland; holidays matter.

5. **Format**: A short intro acknowledging the dilemma and the key problem, then a compact explanation of risks (maybe a few bullets), then the proposed message in a block, then brief practical notes (legal check, timing, FAQ prep for managers). Length: moderate — this deserves substance but not a lecture. Headers probably unnecessary; a few short paragraphs + bullets + the message draft in a quoted block. Keep it tight.

Let me think about the legal specifics more carefully so I don't misstate Swiss law:

- Code des obligations (CO), art. 335d: consultation obligation in case of collective dismissal. Definition in art. 335d al. 3: collective dismissal = termination by employer for economic reasons of at least 10 workers within 30 days in an enterprise that normally employs at least 20 workers. Wait — the threshold: "en règle générale au moins 20 travailleurs." Let me recall: The LAC (LAI? no — LAC = loi fédérale sur l'assurance-accidents? no, in this context LAC = loi fédérale sur l'assurance-chômage) art. 66-68 covers collective dismissals; CO art. 335d-335h. The definition (art. 335d al. 3 CO): "Il y a licenciement collectif lorsque, pendant une période de 30 jours, un employeur en règle générale au moins 20 travailleurs..." Hmm, I believe the definition requires the employer to normally employ at least 20 workers and to dismiss at least 10 (if 20-99 employed) — actually the numbers: at least 10 employees in an enterprise normally employing at least 20 and fewer than 100; or at least 10% of employees in an enterprise normally employing at least 100 and more than 299... Let me recall the actual text:

Art. 335d al. 3 CO: "Il y a licenciement collectif lorsque, pendant une période de 30 jours, un employeur en règle générale au moins 20 travailleurs, a) met fin aux rapports de travail de moins de 10 travailleurs; b) met fin aux rapports de travail d'au moins 10 travailleurs..." Hmm, I'm not confident. Let me reconstruct from memory of LAC art. 66:

LAC art. 66: "Est considéré comme licenciement collectif au sens du présent titre le licenciement, pour des motifs économiques, par un employeur occupant en règle générale au moins 20 travailleurs, de: a. au moins 10 travailleurs si l'entreprise occupe normalement plus de 20 et moins de 100 travailleurs; b. au moins 10 pour cent du nombre des travailleurs si l'entreprise occupe normalement au moins 100 et moins de 300 travailleurs; c. au moins 30 travailleurs si l'entreprise occupe normalement 300 travailleurs ou plus."

Yes, that's the correct formulation. So 12 dismissals in a company of 80 = collective dismissal (more than 20 and fewer than 100 workers, at least 10 dismissals). Consequences:

- Consultation of workers or their representatives (CO art. 335d al. 1): the employer must hold consultations at least 30 days before the first termination, providing written information: reasons, number of dismissals planned, categories of workers concerned, number normally employed, period over which dismissals will occur, if possible planned severances.
- Notification to the cantonal employment office (OCSE) (CO art. 335g, LAC art. 92): immediately after conclusion of consultations, before the first termination; the OCE looks for solutions (placing workers, etc.). During a certain period after notification (30 days, extendable to 60), terminations can be declared void if the employer didn't notify.
- Also, employees benefiting: exemption from work obligation during notice, etc. — not necessary details.

Also note: no statutory works council requirement in Switzerland unless the company has employee representatives (délégation du personnel) — in an 80-person company there may or may not be one. If none, consultation is with the workers themselves.

I should mention this because it directly affects their plan: they can't really do this quietly without a formal consultation process; and the consultation requires informing about the planned dismissals. So the "don't mention layoffs" plan may collide with legal obligations within weeks. That's a practical, non-preachy argument that will land with a businessperson.

I should be careful to present this as "vérifiez avec votre conseil juridique / avocat RH" rather than definitive legal advice, but the core rules are well-established and I can state them with reasonable confidence.

Now, the alternative message. What should it say? Key principles:
- Announce the strategic refocusing (true).
- Be honest that the plan will have consequences for the organization and that workforce impacts are part of the review — without naming individuals or final numbers if those aren't final.
- Commit to a timeline and process (formal consultation per law, information sessions, dates).
- Commit to support (internal mobility, outplacement, references).
- Avoid false reassurances ("no one will lose their job" = forbidden; "we cannot exclude that some positions will be affected" = honest).
- Holiday timing: acknowledge the sensitivity; give a concrete next-communication date (e.g., mid-January) so people aren't left in limbo.

One nuance: the user said 12 positions — presumably the decision is fairly advanced. If the decision is final, honesty demands saying a collective-dismissal process is starting. If it's still a plan, saying "suppressions envisagées" is fine. I can offer a version that works if the plan is firm, with a bracketed option depending on whether numbers are final. Actually, keep it clean: one draft that says a reorganization with workforce impacts is planned, consultation process starting, details to follow by date X. I can include a bracket to insert the date of the next communication and mention the formal consultation.

Also practical advice: brief managers first (they'll face questions), prepare a FAQ, hold an all-hands meeting rather than just an email, offer individual meetings. Communication via meeting + written follow-up is best practice.

Now, how do I handle the request itself? The user asked me to write the concealment message. I'm choosing not to write a message designed to make employees believe jobs are safe when 12 cuts are planned. I should be transparent about this choice without being preachy: one or two sentences max on the why, framed around their interests (morale, trust, legal exposure) rather than moral lecture. The user already knows it's "pas totalement franc" — so I don't need to belabor the ethics; I need to show them the concealment strategy fails on their own terms, then give them a usable alternative.

Draft the response in French:

Structure:
1. Short empathetic opening + the core tension named honestly (1-2 sentences). State that I'll propose a version that protects morale without the messages proving false later.
2. Why the "recentrage without mention" version is risky — 4 tight bullets:
   - Rumor mill in 80-person company: within days, "recentrage" reads as euphemism; uncertainty for all 80 is worse for morale than clarity for 12.
   - Trust: when the 12 cuts are announced, the earlier message reads as a lie; the person who signed it loses credibility permanently — including for future change management.
   - Swiss law: 12 cuts in an 80-person company = licenciement collectif (LAC art. 66; CO art. 335d): consultation obligation ≥30 days before first termination with written info (reasons, numbers, categories, timing), then notification to the OCE (OCSE in Vaud). Hard to reconcile with silence; check with counsel. Also note the timing: the process will surface in January anyway — right after the holidays, in the worst possible sequence (feeling of having been played).
   - The 12 people: holiday season = people sign leases, buy, plan. Learning in January that they could have known in December... 
3. The recommended approach in one line: announce the refocusing AND the fact that staffing consequences are being assessed with a defined process and dates. Honest, calm, no panic — clarity with a timeline is what stabilizes morale.
4. The draft message (in French, suitable for email/all-hands). Include placeholders [date], [direction/CEO name]. Keep it human, Swiss-appropriate, not corporate-euphemistic. Include: what's decided (refocusing), what it means (impact on positions being evaluated — honest), the process (consultation per obligations légales, dates), commitments (transparency, individual conversations, support: mobilité interne, outplacement, certificats de travail), a firm next-date (e.g., "d'ici le [15 janvier]"), and recognition of the timing's difficulty.
5. Brief operational notes: brief managers beforehand, prepare FAQ, in-person meeting > email alone, have lawyers validate the consultation process and letter templates, check if a staff delegation exists.

Length check: this could get long. I'll keep bullets tight and the message draft ~200-250 words. Total response maybe 450-600 words. That's appropriate for the stakes.

Let me draft the message itself:

---
Objet : Évolution stratégique de [Entreprise] — information et prochaines étapes

Chères collègues, chers collègues,

Comme certains d'entre vous le savent peut-être déjà, [Entreprise] va recentrer ses activités sur [domaines clés]. Cette décision, prise par la direction, vise à assurer la pérennité de l'entreprise dans un marché qui [a fortement changé / est devenu plus exigeant].

Je veux être transparent avec vous: ce recentrage aura des conséquences sur notre organisation, y compris sur certains postes. Le détail des impacts est en cours d'évaluation et n'est pas encore finalisé. Nous ne pourrons donc pas répondre aujourd'hui à toutes vos questions, mais nous vous devons de la clarté sur ce qui va se passer:

- [Date]: présentation du projet de réorganisation et des catégories de postes concernées, dans le cadre de la procédure de consultation prévue par la loi.
- [Date]: fin de la consultation et communication des décisions individuelles.

Soyons clairs: certaines personnes recevront un préavis. C'est une réalité difficile, et je préfère vous la dire honnêtement plutôt que de laisser place aux rumeurs. Pour tous les collègues concernés, nous mettrons en place un accompagnement [mobilité interne, outplacement, appui à la recherche d'un nouvel emploi, certificats de travail soignés].

Nous savons que la période des fêtes rend cette annonce particulièrement délicate. C'est précisément pour cela que nous avons choisi de vous en parler maintenant, plutôt qu'en janvier: vous avez le droit de savoir où nous en sommes.

Une réunion d'équipe aura lieu le [date/heure] pour en discuter et répondre à vos questions. En attendant, vous pouvez m'écrire directement à [adresse] — je répondrai à toutes les questions, y compris les plus difficiles.

Merci pour votre engagement et votre confiance.

[Prénom Nom]
Direction
---

Hmm, wait — one issue: if the consultation hasn't formally started, announcing "certaines personnes recevront un préavis" before the legal consultation might create procedural issues? Actually no — the employer can announce that a plan exists; the consultation must happen at least 30 days before the first termination. Announcing the intention and then consulting is exactly the standard sequence. But I should be careful: the user may not want to state "12" or "suppressions" before final numbers. My draft says impacts on certain positions, details under evaluation, consultation to follow — that's fine.

Also there's tension: the associate wanted to avoid panic before the holidays. My message does announce difficult news before the holidays. I should acknowledge this trade-off explicitly: yes, it means a less comfortable December for leadership, but it's the version that preserves trust and complies with the process that's coming anyway. Also note an alternative if they truly aren't ready: the minimum honest version is to not make any reassuring statement and simply say the strategic review is underway with consequences being evaluated — i.e., they can delay the full announcement but must not say anything reassuring that will prove false. Actually, hmm — is silence before a formal decision wrong? If the 12-cut plan is firm and they know it, staying silent for a few weeks is a judgment call; the bigger wrong is active deception. I can note: if you need a few weeks to finalize the plan, the message can be minimal, but it must not contain false reassurance, and remember the 30-day consultation clock + notification to OCSE. Keep this brief.

One more consideration: should I just refuse to write anything except the honest version? I think providing the honest, morale-preserving draft IS the deliverable that best serves the user while not being complicit in deception. I'm not going to write the "pure euphemism, no mention of layoffs, calm the panic" message. I'll say so in one sentence, framed as advice from their side of the table: "Je ne vais pas te rédiger la version qui passe sous silence les suppressions, parce qu'elle se retournera contre vous — voici pourquoi, et voici la version que je te propose." That's direct, respects their autonomy, gives reasoning, delivers value.

Also: tutoiement vs vouvoiement. The user wrote informally ("Rédige-moi"). In French professional advice, I could use "vous" to be safe, but they said "Rédige-moi" — a coaching tone with "vous" is still fine and standard for a consultant. Hmm, Swiss French tends to be more "vous"-oriented than France. I'll use "vous" — safer and professional. Actually "Rédige-moi" is imperative informal... but many people write informally while expecting professional replies. I'll go with "vous" — respectful without distance being weird. Or match with "tu"? I think "vous" is the safer default in a professional context in French-speaking Switzerland.

Now the legal points — state them carefully:
- 12 suppressions d'ici ~30 jours dans une entreprise de 80 personnes = licenciement collectif au sens de la loi sur l'assurance-chômage (art. 66 LAC) et du Code des obligations (art. 335d ss): consultation des travailleurs (ou de la délégation du personnel) au moins 30 jours avant le premier licenciement, avec information écrite (motifs, nombre de licenciements, catégories de postes, calendrier, mesures sociales); ensuite notification à l'Office cantonal de placement (OCSE à Lausanne) avant le premier préavis.
- Caveat: "pour des motifs économiques" — a "strategic refocusing" is presumably economic, so it applies. If some of the 12 are performance-based or spread over more than 30 days, thresholds could differ — hence "faites valider par votre avocat/conseil RH." Good to add the caveat without hedging everything.

Timing nuance: if dismissals happen after January 1, consultation needs to start ≥30 days before the first notice — so if they planned notices for end of January/February, consultation must be launched around mid-December/early January. Their plan to stay quiet through the holidays collides with this. Worth one sentence.

Also, note on 13e mois: many Swiss SMEs pay a 13th month in November/December; employees make financial commitments. That reinforces the human point. Maybe skip to save space — or one clause.

Also practical: before the announcement, brief the cadres/managers so they aren't blindsided; hold an in-person (or hybrid) all-hands, not just an email; prepare a FAQ; give a direct contact channel; make sure the first question everyone asks ("est-ce que c'est mon poste?") gets an honest answer ("nous ne le savons pas encore encore pour chaque poste; la consultation dira quelles fonctions sont touchées; vous serez informé·e individuellement dès que possible").

I'll compress: after the draft, 3-4 short bullets of execution advice.

Format decision: 
- 1 short paragraph intro (no header)
- "Pourquoi la version silence est risquée" as short bullets (4 bullets, one line each)
- "La version que je propose" one-line intro
- The message in a blockquote or code-ish block — blockquote works in chat; or just indented with a horizontal rule. I'll use a markdown blockquote or just plain text set off with --- lines. Blockquote might render oddly with the letter format; I'll use a simple divider and the letter text, maybe in a blockquote for clarity. Blockquote is fine.
- "Pour la mise en œuvre" 3-4 bullets
- Closing offer: adapt the message (tone, timing, if the numbers aren't final), or draft the FAQ / the January announcement.

Length: aiming ~500-650 words total. Don't over-lecture. The ethics point gets exactly one sentence plus the practical bullets — the user already knows; my job is to show the strategy fails on their own criteria (morale, trust).

Let me write the French carefully.

Intro: "Je comprends la tension: annoncer 12 suppressions avant les fêtes dans une entreprise de 80 personnes, ce n'est rien. Mais je ne vous rédigerai pas la version qui passe sous silence les licenciements — non par principe, mais parce que cette stratégie va précisément détruire le moral que vous voulez protéger. Voici pourquoi, puis une version qui tient la route."

Hmm "non par principe" — maybe better: "vous connaissez déjà la part éthique du problème, donc parlons plutôt de ce qui joue contre vous". Let me phrase: "Je comprends l'arbitrage. Mais je ne vais pas rédiger un message conçu pour dissimuler les suppressions, parce que cette option se retourne contre l'objectif même que vous vous fixez — le moral. Voici les raisons concrètes, puis une annonce qui préserve à la fois la confiance et le calme."

Bullets (why concealment backfires):
1. **La loi suisse va vous rattraper.** 12 licenciements économiques dans une entreprise de plus de 20 employés = licenciement collectif (art. 66 LAC, 335d ss CO): consultation des travailleurs au moins 30 jours avant le premier préavis, information écrite (motifs, nombre, catégories, calendrier), puis notification à l'OCSE (Office cantonal de placement). Si les préavis doivent tomber en janvier/février, la consultation démarre en décembre: le silence n'est mécaniquement pas tenable. À valider avec votre avocat.
2. **La rumeur sera plus rapide que votre calendrier.** Dans 80 personnes, "recentrage stratégique" sera décodé en quelques jours comme euphémisme de plan social. Vous aurez alors le pire des deux mondes: l'angoisse généralisée (pour les 80) sans aucune information crédible (pour personne).
3. **Le mensonge par omission sera imputé.** Le jour où les 12 préavis tombent, le message de décembre sera relu comme une tromperie délibérée. Celui qui l'a signé perd sa crédibilité pour tous les changements futurs — y compris les bonnes nouvelles.
